branches.label: sns
branches.shortDescription: Triggers a function when a new message is published to an SNS topic.

properties.name: snsTopicName
properties.shortDescription: The name of an SNS topic defined in your stack's resources.
properties.longDescription: You must specify either snsTopicName or snsTopicArn.

properties.name: snsTopicArn
properties.shortDescription: The ARN of an existing SNS topic.
properties.longDescription: Use this to subscribe to a topic that is not managed by your stack. You must specify either snsTopicName or snsTopicArn.

properties.name: filterPolicy
properties.shortDescription: Filter messages by attributes so only relevant ones trigger the function.
properties.longDescription: Uses SNS subscription filter policy syntax. For content-based filtering, use EventBridge instead.

properties.name: onDeliveryFailure
properties.shortDescription: A destination for messages that fail to be delivered to the target.
properties.longDescription: In rare cases (e.g., if the target function cannot scale fast enough), a message might fail to be delivered. This property specifies an SQS queue where failed messages will be sent.

branches.label: sqs
branches.shortDescription: Triggers a function when new messages are available in an SQS queue.

properties.name: sqsQueueName
properties.shortDescription: The name of an SQS queue defined in your stack's resources.
properties.longDescription: You must specify either sqsQueueName or sqsQueueArn.

properties.name: sqsQueueArn
properties.shortDescription: The ARN of an existing SQS queue.
properties.longDescription: Use this to consume messages from a queue that is not managed by your stack. You must specify either sqsQueueName or sqsQueueArn.

properties.name: batchSize
properties.shortDescription: The maximum number of records to process in a single batch.
properties.longDescription: Maximum is 10,000.

properties.name: maxBatchWindowSeconds
properties.shortDescription: The maximum time (in seconds) to wait before invoking the function with a batch of records.
properties.longDescription: Maximum is 300 seconds. If not set, the function is invoked as soon as messages are available.

branches.label: kinesis-stream
branches.shortDescription: Triggers a function when new records are available in a Kinesis Data Stream.

properties.name: kinesisStreamName
properties.shortDescription: The name of a Kinesis stream defined in your stack's resources.
properties.longDescription: You must specify either kinesisStreamName or streamArn.

properties.name: streamArn
properties.shortDescription: The ARN of an existing Kinesis stream to consume records from.
properties.longDescription: Use this to consume from a stream that is not managed by your stack. You must specify either kinesisStreamName or streamArn.

properties.name: consumerArn
properties.shortDescription: The ARN of a specific stream consumer to use.
properties.longDescription: This cannot be used with autoCreateConsumer.

properties.name: autoCreateConsumer
properties.shortDescription: Automatically creates a dedicated stream consumer for this integration.
properties.longDescription: This is recommended for minimizing latency and maximizing throughput. For more details, see the AWS documentation on stream consumers. This cannot be used with consumerArn.

properties.name: maxBatchWindowSeconds
properties.shortDescription: The maximum time (in seconds) to wait before invoking the function with a batch of records.
properties.longDescription: Maximum is 300 seconds.

properties.name: batchSize
properties.shortDescription: The maximum number of records to process in a single batch.
properties.longDescription: Maximum is 10,000.

properties.name: startingPosition
properties.shortDescription: The position in the stream from which to start reading records.
properties.longDescription:
• LATEST: Read only new records.
  • TRIM_HORIZON: Read all available records from the beginning of the stream.

properties.name: maximumRetryAttempts
properties.shortDescription: The number of times to retry a failed batch of records.
properties.longDescription: Important: If an error occurs, the entire batch is retried, including records that were processed successfully. Your function should be idempotent to handle this.

properties.name: onFailure
properties.shortDescription: A destination (SQS queue or SNS topic) for batches that fail after all retry attempts.

properties.name: parallelizationFactor
properties.shortDescription: The number of batches to process concurrently from the same shard.

properties.name: bisectBatchOnFunctionError
properties.shortDescription: Splits a failed batch in two before retrying.
properties.longDescription: This can be useful if a failure is caused by a batch being too large.

branches.label: dynamo-db-stream
branches.shortDescription: Triggers a function when items are created, updated, or deleted in a DynamoDB table.

properties.name: streamArn
properties.shortDescription: The ARN of the DynamoDB table stream.

properties.name: maxBatchWindowSeconds
properties.shortDescription: The maximum time (in seconds) to wait before invoking the function with a batch of records.
properties.longDescription: Maximum is 300 seconds.

properties.name: batchSize
properties.shortDescription: The maximum number of records to process in a single batch.
properties.longDescription: Maximum is 1,000.

properties.name: startingPosition
properties.shortDescription: The position in the stream from which to start reading records.
properties.longDescription:
• LATEST: Read only new records.
  • TRIM_HORIZON: Read all available records from the beginning of the stream.

properties.name: maximumRetryAttempts
properties.shortDescription: The number of times to retry a failed batch of records.
properties.longDescription: Important: If an error occurs, the entire batch is retried, including records that were processed successfully. Your function should be idempotent to handle this.

properties.name: onFailure
properties.shortDescription: A destination (SQS queue or SNS topic) for batches that fail after all retry attempts.

properties.name: parallelizationFactor
properties.shortDescription: The number of batches to process concurrently from the same shard.

properties.name: bisectBatchOnFunctionError
properties.shortDescription: Splits a failed batch in two before retrying.
properties.longDescription: This can be useful if a failure is caused by a batch being too large.

branches.label: s3
branches.shortDescription: Triggers a function when files are created, deleted, or restored in an S3 bucket.

properties.name: bucketArn
properties.shortDescription: The ARN of the S3 bucket to monitor for events.

properties.name: s3EventType
properties.shortDescription: The type of S3 event that will trigger the function.

properties.name: filterRule
properties.shortDescription: A filter to apply to objects, so the function is only triggered for relevant objects.

branches.label: schedule
branches.shortDescription: Triggers a function on a recurring schedule (cron jobs, periodic tasks).

properties.name: scheduleRate
properties.shortDescription: The schedule rate or cron expression.
properties.longDescription: Examples: rate(2 hours), cron(0 10 * * ? *)

properties.name: input
properties.shortDescription: A fixed JSON object to be passed as the event payload.

properties.name: inputPath
properties.shortDescription: A JSONPath expression to extract a portion of the event to pass to the target.
properties.longDescription: This is useful for forwarding only a specific part of the event payload. You can only use one of input, inputPath, or inputTransformer.

examples.code:
resources:
  reportFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/report.ts
      events:
        - type: schedule
          properties:
            scheduleRate: rate(1 hour)
            # [!code focus-start]
            inputPath: $.detail
            # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: inputTransformer
properties.shortDescription: Customizes the event payload sent to the target.
properties.longDescription: This allows you to extract values from the original event and use them to construct a new payload. You can only use one of input, inputPath, or inputTransformer.

examples.code:
resources:
  reportFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/report.ts
      events:
        - type: schedule
          properties:
            scheduleRate: rate(1 hour)
            # [!code focus-start]
            inputTransformer:
              inputPathsMap:
                eventTime: $.time
              inputTemplate:
                message: This event occurred at <eventTime>.
            # [!code focus-end]

branches.label: cloudwatch-log
branches.shortDescription: Triggers a function when new log records appear in a CloudWatch log group.

properties.name: logGroupArn
properties.shortDescription: The ARN of the log group to watch for new records.

properties.name: filter
properties.shortDescription: A filter pattern to apply to the log records.
properties.longDescription: Only logs that match this pattern will trigger the function. For details on the syntax, see the AWS documentation on filter and pattern syntax.

branches.label: http-api-gateway
branches.shortDescription: Triggers a function when an HTTP API Gateway receives a matching request.

properties.name: httpApiGatewayName
properties.shortDescription: The name of the HTTP API Gateway.

properties.name: method
properties.shortDescription: The HTTP method that will trigger this integration.
properties.longDescription: You can specify an exact method (e.g., GET) or use * to match any method.

properties.name: path
properties.shortDescription: The URL path that will trigger this integration.
properties.longDescription:
• Exact path: /users
  • Path with parameter: /users/{id}. The id will be available in event.pathParameters.id.
  • Greedy path: /files/{proxy+}. This will match any path starting with /files/.

properties.name: authorizer
properties.shortDescription: An authorizer to protect this route.
properties.longDescription: Unauthorized requests will be rejected with a 401 Unauthorized response.

properties.name: userPoolName
properties.shortDescription: Name of the user pool to protect the API
properties.longDescription:
The Stacktape name of the user-auth-pool resource whose tokens should be accepted by this HTTP API authorizer. Stacktape uses this to:

  • Set the expected audience to the user pool client ID.
  • Build the expected issuer URL based on the user pool and AWS region.

In practice this means only JWTs issued by this pool (and its client) will be considered valid.

examples.code:
resources:
  authPool:
    type: user-auth-pool
    properties:
      userVerificationType: email-code
  httpApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /me
            authorizer:
              type: cognito
              properties:
                # [!code focus-start]
                userPoolName: authPool
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: identitySources
properties.shortDescription: Where to read the JWT from in the request
properties.longDescription:
A list of identity sources that tell API Gateway where to look for the bearer token, using the $request.* syntax from API Gateway (for example '$request.header.Authorization').

If you omit this, Stacktape defaults to reading the token from the Authorization HTTP header, using a JWT authorizer as described in the API Gateway v2 authorizer docs (AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer).

examples.code:
resources:
  authPool:
    type: user-auth-pool
    properties:
      userVerificationType: email-code
  httpApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /me
            authorizer:
              type: cognito
              properties:
                userPoolName: authPool
                # [!code focus-start]
                identitySources:
                  - $request.header.Authorization
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: functionName
properties.shortDescription: Name of the authorizer function
properties.longDescription: The Stacktape name of a function resource that should run for each authorized request. API Gateway calls this Lambda, passes request details, and uses its response to allow or deny access.

examples.code:
resources:
  authorizerFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/authorizer.ts
  httpApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /orders
            authorizer:
              type: lambda
              properties:
                # [!code focus-start]
                functionName: authorizerFunction
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: iamResponse
properties.shortDescription: Use IAM-style (v1) authorizer responses
properties.longDescription:
• If true, your Lambda must return a full IAM policy document (the "v1" format).
  • If false or omitted, Stacktape enables simple responses (the HTTP API v2 payload format) so your Lambda can return a small JSON object with an isAuthorized flag and optional context.

This flag is wired to EnableSimpleResponses on the underlying AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer.

examples.code:
resources:
  authorizerFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/authorizer.ts
  httpApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /orders
            authorizer:
              type: lambda
              properties:
                functionName: authorizerFunction
                # [!code focus-start]
                iamResponse: true
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: identitySources
properties.shortDescription: Where to read identity data from
properties.longDescription:
A list of request fields API Gateway should pass into your Lambda authorizer (for example headers, query parameters, or stage variables) using the $request.* syntax.

When left empty, no specific identity sources are configured and your Lambda must inspect the incoming event directly.

examples.code:
resources:
  authorizerFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/authorizer.ts
  httpApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /orders
            authorizer:
              type: lambda
              properties:
                functionName: authorizerFunction
                # [!code focus-start]
                identitySources:
                  - $request.header.Authorization
                  - $request.querystring.apiKey
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: cacheResultSeconds
properties.shortDescription: Cache authorizer results
properties.longDescription:
Number of seconds API Gateway should cache the result of the Lambda authorizer for a given identity. While cached, repeated requests skip calling your authorizer function and reuse the previous result.

This value is applied to AuthorizerResultTtlInSeconds. If omitted, Stacktape sets it to 0 (no caching).

examples.code:
resources:
  authorizerFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/authorizer.ts
  httpApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /orders
            authorizer:
              type: lambda
              properties:
                functionName: authorizerFunction
                identitySources:
                  - $request.header.Authorization
                # [!code focus-start]
                cacheResultSeconds: 300
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: payloadFormat
properties.shortDescription: The payload format version for the Lambda integration.
properties.longDescription: For details on the differences between formats, see the AWS documentation.

branches.label: event-bus
branches.shortDescription: Triggers a batch job when an event matching a specified pattern is received by an event bus.

properties.name: eventBusArn
properties.shortDescription: The ARN of an existing event bus.
properties.longDescription: Use this to subscribe to an event bus that is not managed by your stack. You must specify only one of eventBusArn, eventBusName, or useDefaultBus.

properties.name: eventBusName
properties.shortDescription: The name of an event bus defined in your stack's resources.
properties.longDescription: You must specify only one of eventBusArn, eventBusName, or useDefaultBus.

properties.name: useDefaultBus
properties.shortDescription: Uses the default AWS event bus.
properties.longDescription: You must specify only one of eventBusArn, eventBusName, or useDefaultBus.

properties.name: eventPattern
properties.shortDescription: A pattern to filter events from the event bus.
properties.longDescription: Only events that match this pattern will trigger the target. For details on the syntax, see the AWS EventBridge documentation on event patterns.

properties.name: onDeliveryFailure
properties.shortDescription: A destination for events that fail to be delivered to the target.
properties.longDescription: In rare cases, an event might fail to be delivered. This property specifies an SQS queue where failed events will be sent.

properties.name: input
properties.shortDescription: A fixed JSON object to be passed as the event payload.

properties.name: inputPath
properties.shortDescription: A JSONPath expression to extract a portion of the event to pass to the target.
properties.longDescription: This is useful for forwarding only a specific part of the event payload. You can only use one of input, inputPath, or inputTransformer.

examples.code:
resources:
  orderEvents:
    type: event-bus
  orderProcessor:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/process-order.ts
      events:
        - type: event-bus
          properties:
            eventBusName: orderEvents
            eventPattern:
              source:
                - my.orders
            # [!code focus-start]
            inputPath: $.detail
            # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: inputTransformer
properties.shortDescription: Customizes the event payload sent to the target.
properties.longDescription: This allows you to extract values from the original event and use them to construct a new payload. You can only use one of input, inputPath, or inputTransformer.

examples.code:
resources:
  orderEvents:
    type: event-bus
  orderProcessor:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/process-order.ts
      events:
        - type: event-bus
          properties:
            eventBusName: orderEvents
            eventPattern:
              source:
                - my.orders
            # [!code focus-start]
            inputTransformer:
              inputPathsMap:
                instanceId: $.detail.instance-id
                instanceState: $.detail.state
              inputTemplate:
                message: Instance <instanceId> is now in state <instanceState>.
            # [!code focus-end]

resources:
  uploadProcessor:
    type: batch-job
    properties:
      container:
        packaging:
          type: stacktape-image-buildpack
          properties:
            entryfilePath: src/onUpload.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 2
        memory: 3840
      # [!code focus-start]
      events:
        - type: s3
          properties:
            bucketArn: $ResourceParam('uploadsBucket', 'arn')
            s3EventType: 's3:ObjectCreated:*'
        - type: schedule
          properties:
            scheduleRate: rate(1 hour)
      # [!code focus-end]
      connectTo:
        - uploadsBucket
  uploadsBucket:
    type: bucket

properties.name: iamRoleStatements
properties.shortDescription: Raw IAM policy statements for permissions not covered by connectTo.
properties.longDescription: Added as a separate policy alongside auto-generated permissions. Use this for accessing AWS services directly (e.g., Rekognition, Textract, Bedrock).

examples.code:
resources:
  processor:
    type: batch-job
    properties:
      container:
        packaging:
          type: stacktape-image-buildpack
          properties:
            entryfilePath: src/job.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 1
        memory: 2048
      # [!code focus-start]
      iamRoleStatements:
        - Effect: Allow
          Action:
            - textract:AnalyzeDocument
          Resource:
            - '*'
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: logging
properties.shortDescription: Container logging (stdout/stderr). Sent to CloudWatch, viewable with stacktape logs.

examples.code:
resources:
  reportGenerator:
    type: batch-job
    properties:
      container:
        packaging:
          type: stacktape-image-buildpack
          properties:
            entryfilePath: src/report.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 1
        memory: 1920
      # [!code focus-start]
      logging:
        retentionDays: 30
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: retryConfig
properties.shortDescription: Auto-retry on failure, timeout, or Spot interruption.

examples.code:
resources:
  flakyJob:
    type: batch-job
    properties:
      container:
        packaging:
          type: stacktape-image-buildpack
          properties:
            entryfilePath: src/job.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 2
        memory: 3840
      # [!code focus-start]
      retryConfig:
        attempts: 4
        retryIntervalSeconds: 5
        retryIntervalMultiplier: 2
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: timeout
properties.shortDescription: Max run time in seconds. The job is killed if it exceeds this, then retried if retryConfig is set.

examples.code:
resources:
  dataImporter:
    type: batch-job
    properties:
      container:
        packaging:
          type: stacktape-image-buildpack
          properties:
            entryfilePath: src/import.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 2
        memory: 3840
      # [!code focus-start]
      timeout: 3600
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: useSpotInstances
properties.shortDescription: Use discounted spare AWS capacity. Saves up to 90%, but jobs can be interrupted.
properties.longDescription:
Use this when: Your job can safely be restarted from the beginning (e.g., data imports, image processing, ML training with checkpoints). Combine with retryConfig to auto-retry on interruption.

Don't use when: Your job has side effects that can't be repeated (e.g., sending emails, charging payments) or must finish within a strict deadline.

If interrupted, your container gets a SIGTERM and 120 seconds to shut down gracefully.

examples.code:
resources:
  mlTrainer:
    type: batch-job
    properties:
      container:
        packaging:
          type: stacktape-image-buildpack
          properties:
            entryfilePath: src/train.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 4
        memory: 15360
        gpu: 1
      # [!code focus-start]
      useSpotInstances: true
      # [!code focus-end]
      retryConfig:
        attempts: 3

properties.name: cpu
properties.shortDescription: Number of vCPUs for the job (e.g., 1, 2, 4).

examples.code:
resources:
  computeJob:
    type: batch-job
    properties:
      container:
        packaging:
          type: stacktape-image-buildpack
          properties:
            entryfilePath: src/compute.ts
      resources:
        # [!code focus-start]
        cpu: 4
        # [!code focus-end]
        memory: 7680

properties.name: memory
properties.shortDescription: Memory in MB. Use slightly less than powers of 2 for efficient instance sizing.
properties.longDescription: AWS reserves some memory for system processes. Requesting exactly 8192 MB (8 GB) may provision a larger instance than needed. Use 7680 MB instead to fit on a standard 8 GB instance.

examples.code:
resources:
  memoryJob:
    type: batch-job
    properties:
      container:
        packaging:
          type: stacktape-image-buildpack
          properties:
            entryfilePath: src/compute.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 2
        # [!code focus-start]
        memory: 7680
        # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: gpu
properties.shortDescription: Number of GPUs. The job will run on a GPU instance (NVIDIA A100, A10G, etc.).
properties.longDescription: Omit for CPU-only workloads.

examples.code:
resources:
  inferenceJob:
    type: batch-job
    properties:
      container:
        packaging:
          type: stacktape-image-buildpack
          properties:
            entryfilePath: src/infer.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 4
        memory: 15360
        # [!code focus-start]
        gpu: 1
        # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: attempts
properties.shortDescription: Max retry attempts before the job is marked as failed.

examples.code:
resources:
  batchProcessor:
    type: batch-job
    properties:
      container:
        packaging:
          type: stacktape-image-buildpack
          properties:
            entryfilePath: src/process.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 2
        memory: 3840
      retryConfig:
        # [!code focus-start]
        attempts: 3
        # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: retryIntervalMultiplier
properties.shortDescription: Multiply wait time by this factor after each retry (exponential backoff).
properties.longDescription: E.g., with retryIntervalSeconds: 5 and retryIntervalMultiplier: 2, waits are 5s, 10s, 20s, etc.

examples.code:
resources:
  batchProcessor:
    type: batch-job
    properties:
      container:
        packaging:
          type: stacktape-image-buildpack
          properties:
            entryfilePath: src/process.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 2
        memory: 3840
      retryConfig:
        attempts: 4
        retryIntervalSeconds: 5
        # [!code focus-start]
        retryIntervalMultiplier: 2
        # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: retryIntervalSeconds
properties.shortDescription: Seconds to wait between retries.

examples.code:
resources:
  batchProcessor:
    type: batch-job
    properties:
      container:
        packaging:
          type: stacktape-image-buildpack
          properties:
            entryfilePath: src/process.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 2
        memory: 3840
      retryConfig:
        attempts: 3
        # [!code focus-start]
        retryIntervalSeconds: 10
        # [!code focus-end]

Bucket.shortDescription: S3 storage bucket for files, images, backups, or any binary data.

properties.name: overrides
properties.shortDescription: Escape hatch to modify the underlying CloudFormation resources Stacktape creates.
properties.longDescription: Use dot-notation paths to override specific properties on any child resource. Find resource logical IDs with stacktape info:stack.

examples.code:
resources:
  mainDb:
    type: relational-database
    properties:
      credentials:
        masterUserPassword: $Secret('db-password')
      engine:
        type: postgres
        properties:
          version: '16.2'
          primaryInstance:
            instanceSize: db.t3.micro
    # [!code focus-start]
    overrides:
      MainDbDatabaseInstance:
        Properties.StorageEncrypted: true
    # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: accessibilityMode
properties.shortDescription: Configures pre-defined accessibility modes for the bucket.
properties.longDescription:
This allows you to easily configure the most common access patterns.

Available modes:

  • public-read-write: Everyone can read from and write to the bucket.
  • public-read: Everyone can read from the bucket. Only compute resources and entities with sufficient IAM permissions can write to it.
  • private (default): Only compute resources and entities with sufficient IAM permissions can read from or write to the bucket.

For functions, batch jobs, and container workloads, you can grant the required IAM permissions using the allowsAccessTo or iamRoleStatements properties in their respective configurations.

examples.code:
resources:
  myBucket:
    type: bucket
    properties:
      accessibility:
        # [!code focus-start]
        accessibilityMode: public-read
        # [!code focus-end]
      cors:
        enabled: true

properties.name: accessPolicyStatements
properties.shortDescription: Advanced access configuration that leverages IAM policy statements.
properties.longDescription: This gives you fine-grained access control over the bucket.

examples.code:
resources:
  myBucket:
    type: bucket
    properties:
      accessibility:
        accessibilityMode: private
        # [!code focus-start]
        accessPolicyStatements:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: '*'
            Action:
              - 's3:GetObject'
            Resource:
              - $Format('{}/public/*', $ResourceParam('myBucket', 'arn'))
        # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: enabled
properties.shortDescription: Enable CDN (CloudFront) for faster global delivery and lower bandwidth costs.
properties.longDescription: Caches responses at edge locations worldwide so users get content from the nearest server. The CDN itself has no monthly fee — you pay per request (~$0.01/10k) and per GB transferred.

examples.code:
resources:
assets:
  type: bucket
  properties:
    directoryUpload:
      directoryPath: ./public
    cdn:
      # [!code focus-start]
      enabled: true
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: cachingOptions
properties.shortDescription: Control how long and what gets cached at the CDN edge.
properties.longDescription:
When the origin response has no Cache-Control header, defaults apply:

  • Bucket origins: cached for 6 months (or until invalidated on deploy).
  • API Gateway / Load Balancer origins: not cached.

examples.code:
resources:
assets:
  type: bucket
  properties:
    directoryUpload:
      directoryPath: ./public
    cdn:
      enabled: true
      # [!code focus-start]
      cachingOptions:
        defaultTTL: 86400
        maxTTL: 31536000
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: cloudfrontPriceClass
properties.shortDescription: Which regions the CDN serves from. Fewer regions = lower cost, but slower for distant users.
properties.longDescription:
• PriceClass_100: North America + Europe. Cheapest option. Good if your users are in the US/EU.
  • PriceClass_200: Adds Asia, Middle East, Africa.
  • PriceClass_All (default): All regions worldwide, including South America and Oceania.

The CDN itself has no monthly base cost - you only pay per request and per GB transferred. The price class controls which edge locations are used, and some regions cost more per request.

examples.code:
resources:
assets:
  type: bucket
  properties:
    directoryUpload:
      directoryPath: ./public
    cdn:
      enabled: true
      # [!code focus-start]
      cloudfrontPriceClass: PriceClass_100
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: customDomains
properties.shortDescription: Custom domains (e.g., cdn.example.com). Stacktape auto-creates DNS records and TLS certificates.
properties.longDescription: Your domain must be added as a Route53 hosted zone in your AWS account first.

examples.code:
resources:
assets:
  type: bucket
  properties:
    directoryUpload:
      directoryPath: ./public
    cdn:
      enabled: true
      # [!code focus-start]
      customDomains:
        - domainName: cdn.example.com
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: defaultRoutePrefix
properties.shortDescription: Prepend a path prefix to all requests forwarded to the origin.
properties.longDescription: E.g., with prefix /v2, a request for /users is forwarded to the origin as /v2/users.

examples.code:
resources:
api:
  type: http-api-gateway
  properties:
    cdn:
      enabled: true
      # [!code focus-start]
      defaultRoutePrefix: /v2
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: disableInvalidationAfterDeploy
properties.shortDescription: Skip clearing the CDN cache after each deploy.
properties.longDescription: By default, all cached content is flushed on every deploy so users see the latest version. Set to true if you manage cache invalidation yourself or want to keep cached content between deploys.

examples.code:
resources:
assets:
  type: bucket
  properties:
    directoryUpload:
      directoryPath: ./public
    cdn:
      enabled: true
      # [!code focus-start]
      disableInvalidationAfterDeploy: true
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: disableUrlNormalization
properties.shortDescription: Disables URL normalization.
properties.longDescription: URL normalization is enabled by default and is useful for serving HTML files from the bucket with clean URLs.

examples.code:
resources:
  assetsBucket:
    type: bucket
    properties:
      directoryUpload:
        directoryPath: ./dist
      cdn:
        enabled: true
        # [!code focus-start]
        disableUrlNormalization: true
        # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: edgeFunctions
properties.shortDescription: Run edge functions on CDN requests/responses (URL rewrites, auth, A/B testing).
properties.longDescription:
• onRequest: Before cache lookup — modify the request, add auth, or return early.
  • onResponse: Before returning to the client — modify headers, add cookies.

examples.code:
resources:
authAtEdge:
  type: edge-lambda-function
  properties:
    packaging:
      type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
      properties:
        entryfilePath: ./src/edge/auth.ts
api:
  type: http-api-gateway
  properties:
    cdn:
      enabled: true
      # [!code focus-start]
      edgeFunctions:
        onRequest: authAtEdge
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: errorDocument
properties.shortDescription: Page to show for 404 errors (e.g., /error.html).

examples.code:
resources:
webapp:
  type: bucket
  properties:
    directoryUpload:
      directoryPath: ./dist
    cdn:
      enabled: true
      # [!code focus-start]
      errorDocument: /error.html
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: forwardingOptions
properties.shortDescription: Control which headers, cookies, and query params are forwarded to your origin.
properties.longDescription: By default, all headers/cookies/query params are forwarded. Use this to restrict what reaches your app (e.g., strip cookies for static content).

examples.code:
resources:
api:
  type: http-api-gateway
  properties:
    cdn:
      enabled: true
      # [!code focus-start]
      forwardingOptions:
        cookies:
          none: true
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: indexDocument
properties.shortDescription: Page served for requests to /.

examples.code:
resources:
webapp:
  type: bucket
  properties:
    directoryUpload:
      directoryPath: ./dist
    cdn:
      enabled: true
      # [!code focus-start]
      indexDocument: /index.html
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: rewriteRoutesForSinglePageApp
properties.shortDescription: Rewrites incoming requests to work for a single-page application.
properties.longDescription:
The routing works as follows:

  • If the path has an extension (e.g., .css, .js, .png), the request is not rewritten, and the appropriate file is returned.
  • If the path does not have an extension, the request is routed to index.html.

This allows single-page applications to handle routing on the client side.

examples.code:
resources:
  assetsBucket:
    type: bucket
    properties:
      directoryUpload:
        directoryPath: ./dist
        headersPreset: single-page-app
      cdn:
        enabled: true
        # [!code focus-start]
        rewriteRoutesForSinglePageApp: true
        # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: routeRewrites
properties.shortDescription: Route specific URL patterns to different origins (e.g., /api/* → Lambda, /assets/* → S3).
properties.longDescription: Evaluated in order; first match wins. Unmatched requests go to the default origin. Each route can have its own caching and forwarding settings.

examples.code:
resources:
api:
  type: http-api-gateway
  properties:
    cdn:
      enabled: true
      # [!code focus-start]
      routeRewrites:
        - path: /assets/*
          routeTo:
            type: bucket
            properties:
              bucketName: assets
      # [!code focus-end]
assets:
  type: bucket
  properties:
    directoryUpload:
      directoryPath: ./public

properties.name: useFirewall
properties.shortDescription: Name of a web-app-firewall resource to protect this CDN from common web exploits.

examples.code:
resources:
cdnFirewall:
  type: web-app-firewall
  properties:
    scope: cdn
api:
  type: http-api-gateway
  properties:
    cdn:
      enabled: true
      # [!code focus-start]
      useFirewall: cdnFirewall
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: enabled
properties.shortDescription: Enable CORS. When true with no rules, uses permissive defaults (* origins, all methods).

examples.code:
resources:
  myBucket:
    type: bucket
    properties:
      # [!code focus-start]
      cors:
        enabled: true
      # [!code focus-end]
      accessibility:
        accessibilityMode: public-read

properties.name: corsRules
properties.shortDescription: Custom CORS rules. First matching rule wins for each preflight request.

examples.code:
resources:
  myBucket:
    type: bucket
    properties:
      cors:
        enabled: true
        # [!code focus-start]
        corsRules:
          - allowedOrigins:
              - 'https://example.com'
            allowedMethods:
              - GET
              - PUT
        # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: allowedHeaders
properties.shortDescription: Allowed request headers.

examples.code:
resources:
  myBucket:
    type: bucket
    properties:
      cors:
        enabled: true
        corsRules:
          - allowedOrigins:
              - 'https://app.example.com'
            allowedMethods:
              - PUT
            # [!code focus-start]
            allowedHeaders:
              - 'Content-Type'
              - 'Authorization'
            # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: allowedMethods
properties.shortDescription: Allowed HTTP methods.

examples.code:
resources:
  myBucket:
    type: bucket
    properties:
      cors:
        enabled: true
        corsRules:
          - allowedOrigins:
              - 'https://app.example.com'
            # [!code focus-start]
            allowedMethods:
              - GET
              - PUT
              - POST
              - DELETE
            # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: allowedOrigins
properties.shortDescription: Allowed origins (e.g., https://example.com). Use * for any.

examples.code:
resources:
  myBucket:
    type: bucket
    properties:
      cors:
        enabled: true
        corsRules:
          # [!code focus-start]
          - allowedOrigins:
              - 'https://app.example.com'
              - 'https://admin.example.com'
          # [!code focus-end]
            allowedMethods:
              - GET

properties.name: exposedResponseHeaders
properties.shortDescription: Response headers accessible to browser JavaScript.

examples.code:
resources:
  myBucket:
    type: bucket
    properties:
      cors:
        enabled: true
        corsRules:
          - allowedOrigins:
              - 'https://app.example.com'
            allowedMethods:
              - GET
            # [!code focus-start]
            exposedResponseHeaders:
              - 'ETag'
              - 'x-amz-request-id'
            # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: maxAge
properties.shortDescription: How long (seconds) browsers can cache preflight responses.

examples.code:
resources:
  myBucket:
    type: bucket
    properties:
      cors:
        enabled: true
        corsRules:
          - allowedOrigins:
              - 'https://app.example.com'
            allowedMethods:
              - GET
            # [!code focus-start]
            maxAge: 3600
            # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: Resource
properties.shortDescription: ARNs of the AWS resources this statement applies to. Use "*" for all resources.

examples.code:
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-image-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
      # [!code focus-start]
      iamRoleStatements:
        - Resource:
            - '*'
          Action:
            - rekognition:DetectLabels
            - rekognition:DetectText
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: Action
properties.shortDescription: AWS actions to allow or deny (e.g., s3:GetObject, sqs:SendMessage).

properties.name: Condition
properties.shortDescription: Conditions under which this statement applies (e.g., IP restrictions, tag-based access).
properties.longDescription:
**Example (YAML):**

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-image-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
      iamRoleStatements:
        - Effect: Allow
          Action:
            - s3:GetObject
          Resource:
            - 'arn:aws:s3:::my-secure-bucket/*'
          Condition:
            Bool:
              'aws:SecureTransport': 'true'
```

**Example (TypeScript):**

```ts
import { WebService, StacktapeImageBuildpackPackaging, defineConfig } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new WebService({
    packaging: new StacktapeImageBuildpackPackaging({ entryfilePath: 'src/server.ts' }),
    resources: { cpu: 0.25, memory: 512 },
    iamRoleStatements: [
      {
        Effect: 'Allow',
        Action: ['s3:GetObject'],
        Resource: ['arn:aws:s3:::my-secure-bucket/*'],
        Condition: { Bool: { 'aws:SecureTransport': 'true' } }
      }
    ]
  });

  return { resources: { api } };
});
```

properties.name: userPoolName
properties.shortDescription: Name of the user pool to protect the API
properties.longDescription:
The Stacktape name of the user-auth-pool resource whose tokens should be accepted by this HTTP API authorizer. Stacktape uses this to:

  • Set the expected audience to the user pool client ID.
  • Build the expected issuer URL based on the user pool and AWS region.

In practice this means only JWTs issued by this pool (and its client) will be considered valid.

    properties:
      userVerificationType: email-code
  httpApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /me
            authorizer:
              type: cognito
              properties:
                # [!code focus-start]
                userPoolName: authPool
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: identitySources
properties.shortDescription: Where to read the JWT from in the request
properties.longDescription:
A list of identity sources that tell API Gateway where to look for the bearer token, using the $request.* syntax from API Gateway (for example '$request.header.Authorization').

If you omit this, Stacktape defaults to reading the token from the Authorization HTTP header, using a JWT authorizer as described in the API Gateway v2 authorizer docs (AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer).

  authPool:

    properties:

  httpApi:

    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /me
            authorizer:
              type: cognito
              properties:
                userPoolName: authPool
                # [!code focus-start]
                identitySources:
                  - $request.header.Authorization
                # [!code focus-end]

branches.label: http-api-gateway
branches.shortDescription: Triggers a container when an HTTP API Gateway receives a matching request.

properties.name: containerPort
properties.shortDescription: The container port that will receive traffic from the API Gateway.

examples.code:
resources:
  publicApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
    properties: {}
  appWorkload:

    properties:

        cpu: 0.5

        - name: web
          packaging:

              image: 'my-org/web-app:latest'
          events:
            - type: http-api-gateway

                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: httpApiGatewayName
properties.shortDescription: The name of the HTTP API Gateway.

properties.name: method
properties.shortDescription: The HTTP method that will trigger this integration.
properties.longDescription: You can specify an exact method (e.g., GET) or use * to match any method.

properties.name: path
properties.shortDescription: The URL path that will trigger this integration.
properties.longDescription:
• Exact path: /users
  • Path with parameter: /users/{id}. The id will be available in event.pathParameters.id.
  • Greedy path: /files/{proxy+}. This will match any path starting with /files/.

properties.name: authorizer
properties.shortDescription: An authorizer to protect this route.
properties.longDescription: Unauthorized requests will be rejected with a 401 Unauthorized response.

properties.name: userPoolName
properties.shortDescription: Name of the user pool to protect the API
properties.longDescription:
The Stacktape name of the user-auth-pool resource whose tokens should be accepted by this HTTP API authorizer. Stacktape uses this to:

  • Set the expected audience to the user pool client ID.
  • Build the expected issuer URL based on the user pool and AWS region.

In practice this means only JWTs issued by this pool (and its client) will be considered valid.

examples.code:
resources:
  authPool:
    type: user-auth-pool
    properties:
      userVerificationType: email-code
  httpApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /me
            authorizer:
              type: cognito
              properties:
                # [!code focus-start]
                userPoolName: authPool
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: identitySources
properties.shortDescription: Where to read the JWT from in the request
properties.longDescription:
A list of identity sources that tell API Gateway where to look for the bearer token, using the $request.* syntax from API Gateway (for example '$request.header.Authorization').

If you omit this, Stacktape defaults to reading the token from the Authorization HTTP header, using a JWT authorizer as described in the API Gateway v2 authorizer docs (AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer).

examples.code:
resources:
  authPool:
    type: user-auth-pool
    properties:
      userVerificationType: email-code
  httpApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /me
            authorizer:
              type: cognito
              properties:
                userPoolName: authPool
                # [!code focus-start]
                identitySources:
                  - $request.header.Authorization
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: functionName
properties.shortDescription: Name of the authorizer function
properties.longDescription: The Stacktape name of a function resource that should run for each authorized request. API Gateway calls this Lambda, passes request details, and uses its response to allow or deny access.

examples.code:
resources:
  authorizerFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack

            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /orders
            authorizer:
              type: lambda
              properties:
                # [!code focus-start]
                functionName: authorizerFunction
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: iamResponse
properties.shortDescription: Use IAM-style (v1) authorizer responses
properties.longDescription:
• If true, your Lambda must return a full IAM policy document (the "v1" format).
  • If false or omitted, Stacktape enables simple responses (the HTTP API v2 payload format) so your Lambda can return a small JSON object with an isAuthorized flag and optional context.

This flag is wired to EnableSimpleResponses on the underlying AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer.

examples.code:
resources:
  authorizerFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/authorizer.ts

  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:

        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /orders
            authorizer:
              type: lambda
              properties:
                functionName: authorizerFunction
                # [!code focus-start]
                iamResponse: true
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: identitySources
properties.shortDescription: Where to read identity data from
properties.longDescription:
A list of request fields API Gateway should pass into your Lambda authorizer (for example headers, query parameters, or stage variables) using the $request.* syntax.

When left empty, no specific identity sources are configured and your Lambda must inspect the incoming event directly.

examples.code:
resources:
  authorizerFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/authorizer.ts

  apiFunction:

    properties:

            method: GET
            path: /orders

              type: lambda
              properties:
                functionName: authorizerFunction
                # [!code focus-start]
                identitySources:
                  - $request.header.Authorization
                  - $request.querystring.apiKey
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: cacheResultSeconds
properties.shortDescription: Cache authorizer results
properties.longDescription:
Number of seconds API Gateway should cache the result of the Lambda authorizer for a given identity. While cached, repeated requests skip calling your authorizer function and reuse the previous result.

This value is applied to AuthorizerResultTtlInSeconds. If omitted, Stacktape sets it to 0 (no caching).

                # [!code focus-start]

ContainerWorkloadHttpApiIntegration.shortDescription: Triggers a container when an HTTP API Gateway receives a matching request.

properties.name: containerPort
properties.shortDescription: The container port that will receive traffic from the API Gateway.

examples.code:
resources:
  publicApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
    properties: {}
  appWorkload:
    type: multi-container-workload
    properties:
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 1024
      containers:
        - name: web
          packaging:
            type: prebuilt-image
            properties:
              image: 'my-org/web-app:latest'
          events:
            - type: http-api-gateway
              properties:
                httpApiGatewayName: publicApi
                method: '*'
                path: '/{proxy+}'
                # [!code focus-start]
                containerPort: 8080
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: httpApiGatewayName
properties.shortDescription: The name of the HTTP API Gateway.

properties.name: method
properties.shortDescription: The HTTP method that will trigger this integration.
properties.longDescription: You can specify an exact method (e.g., GET) or use * to match any method.

properties.name: path
properties.shortDescription: The URL path that will trigger this integration.
properties.longDescription:
• Exact path: /users
  • Path with parameter: /users/{id}. The id will be available in event.pathParameters.id.
  • Greedy path: /files/{proxy+}. This will match any path starting with /files/.

properties.name: authorizer
properties.shortDescription: An authorizer to protect this route.
properties.longDescription: Unauthorized requests will be rejected with a 401 Unauthorized response.

properties.name: userPoolName
properties.shortDescription: Name of the user pool to protect the API
properties.longDescription:
The Stacktape name of the user-auth-pool resource whose tokens should be accepted by this HTTP API authorizer. Stacktape uses this to:

  • Set the expected audience to the user pool client ID.
  • Build the expected issuer URL based on the user pool and AWS region.

In practice this means only JWTs issued by this pool (and its client) will be considered valid.

examples.code:
resources:
  authPool:
    type: user-auth-pool
    properties:
      userVerificationType: email-code
  httpApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /me
            authorizer:
              type: cognito
              properties:
                # [!code focus-start]
                userPoolName: authPool
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: identitySources
properties.shortDescription: Where to read the JWT from in the request
properties.longDescription:
A list of identity sources that tell API Gateway where to look for the bearer token, using the $request.* syntax from API Gateway (for example '$request.header.Authorization').

If you omit this, Stacktape defaults to reading the token from the Authorization HTTP header, using a JWT authorizer as described in the API Gateway v2 authorizer docs (AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer).

examples.code:
resources:
  authPool:
    type: user-auth-pool
    properties:
      userVerificationType: email-code
  httpApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /me
            authorizer:
              type: cognito
              properties:
                userPoolName: authPool
                # [!code focus-start]
                identitySources:
                  - $request.header.Authorization
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: functionName
properties.shortDescription: Name of the authorizer function
properties.longDescription: The Stacktape name of a function resource that should run for each authorized request. API Gateway calls this Lambda, passes request details, and uses its response to allow or deny access.

examples.code:
resources:
  authorizerFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/authorizer.ts
  httpApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /orders
            authorizer:
              type: lambda
              properties:
                # [!code focus-start]
                functionName: authorizerFunction
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: iamResponse
properties.shortDescription: Use IAM-style (v1) authorizer responses
properties.longDescription:
• If true, your Lambda must return a full IAM policy document (the "v1" format).
  • If false or omitted, Stacktape enables simple responses (the HTTP API v2 payload format) so your Lambda can return a small JSON object with an isAuthorized flag and optional context.

This flag is wired to EnableSimpleResponses on the underlying AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer.

examples.code:
resources:
  authorizerFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/authorizer.ts
  httpApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /orders
            authorizer:
              type: lambda
              properties:
                functionName: authorizerFunction
                # [!code focus-start]
                iamResponse: true
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: identitySources
properties.shortDescription: Where to read identity data from
properties.longDescription:
A list of request fields API Gateway should pass into your Lambda authorizer (for example headers, query parameters, or stage variables) using the $request.* syntax.

When left empty, no specific identity sources are configured and your Lambda must inspect the incoming event directly.

examples.code:
resources:
  authorizerFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/authorizer.ts
  httpApi:
    type: http-api-gateway
  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      events:
        - type: http-api-gateway
          properties:
            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /orders
            authorizer:
              type: lambda
              properties:
                functionName: authorizerFunction
                # [!code focus-start]
                identitySources:
                  - $request.header.Authorization
                  - $request.querystring.apiKey
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: cacheResultSeconds
properties.shortDescription: Cache authorizer results
properties.longDescription:
Number of seconds API Gateway should cache the result of the Lambda authorizer for a given identity. While cached, repeated requests skip calling your authorizer function and reuse the previous result.

This value is applied to AuthorizerResultTtlInSeconds. If omitted, Stacktape sets it to 0 (no caching).

    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/authorizer.ts

  apiFunction:
    type: function
    properties:

        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack

            httpApiGatewayName: httpApi
            method: GET
            path: /orders
            authorizer:
              type: lambda
              properties:
                functionName: authorizerFunction
                identitySources:
                  - $request.header.Authorization
                # [!code focus-start]
                cacheResultSeconds: 300
                # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: connectTo
properties.shortDescription: Give this resource access to other resources in your stack.
properties.longDescription:
List the names of resources this workload needs to communicate with. Stacktape automatically:

  • Grants IAM permissions (e.g., S3 read/write, SQS send/receive)
  • Opens network access (security group rules for databases, Redis)
  • Injects environment variables with connection details: STP_[RESOURCE_NAME]_[PARAM]

Example: connectTo: ["myDatabase", "myBucket"] gives this workload full access to both resources and injects STP_MY_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING, STP_MY_BUCKET_NAME, etc.

What each resource type provides:

Bucket — read/write/delete objects → NAME, ARN

DynamoDbTable — CRUD + scan/query → NAME, ARN, STREAM_ARN

RelationalDatabase — network access + connection details → CONNECTION_STRING, HOST, PORT. Aurora also gets READER_CONNECTION_STRING, READER_HOST.

MongoDbAtlasCluster — temporary credential-less access → CONNECTION_STRING

RedisCluster — network access → HOST, READER_HOST, PORT

Function — invoke permission → ARN

BatchJob — submit/list/terminate → JOB_DEFINITION_ARN, STATE_MACHINE_ARN

EventBus — publish events → ARN

UserAuthPool — full control → ID, CLIENT_ID, ARN

SqsQueue — send/receive/delete → ARN, NAME, URL

SnsTopic — publish/subscribe → ARN, NAME

UpstashRedis → HOST, PORT, PASSWORD, REST_TOKEN, REST_URL, REDIS_URL

PrivateService → ADDRESS

aws:ses — full SES email sending permissions

examples.code:
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-image-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 1024
      # [!code focus-start]
      connectTo:
        - mainDb
        - uploads
      # [!code focus-end]
  mainDb:
    type: relational-database
    properties:
      credentials:
        masterUserPassword: $Secret('db-password')
      engine:
        type: postgres
        properties:
          version: '16.2'
          primaryInstance:
            instanceSize: db.t4g.micro
  uploads:
    type: bucket
    properties: {}

      MainDbDatabaseInstance:
        Properties.StorageEncrypted: true
    # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: enableRemoteSessions
properties.shortDescription: Allow SSH-like sessions into the running backend container for debugging.
properties.longDescription: Stacktape enables ECS Exec for Convex internally because it is required to generate the managed admin key after the backend starts. This property is kept for compatibility with generic workload controls and may be removed in a future Convex resource revision.

examples.code:
resources:
  backend:
    type: convex
    properties:
      appDirectory: ./convex
      backend:
        # [!code focus-start]
        enableRemoteSessions: true
        # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: image
properties.shortDescription: Pinned Convex backend Docker image.
properties.longDescription:
Defaults to a known-good version pinned by Stacktape (currently from ghcr.io/get-convex/convex-backend). Override to test newer/older versions. Image upgrades trigger Convex's in-place migration path.

Example: image: 'ghcr.io/get-convex/convex-backend:0a8d9ae0f0e5c6c9c0c0c0c0'

examples.code:
resources:
  backend:
    type: convex
    properties:
      appDirectory: ./convex
      backend:
        # [!code focus-start]
        image: ghcr.io/get-convex/convex-backend:0a8d9ae0f0e5c6c9c0c0c0c0
        # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: logging
properties.shortDescription: Logging configuration for the backend container.
properties.longDescription: Container stdout/stderr are sent to CloudWatch and retained for 90 days by default. View logs with stacktape logs <resourceName>.

examples.code:
resources:
  backend:
    type: convex
    properties:
      appDirectory: ./convex
      backend:
        # [!code focus-start]
        logging:
          retentionDays: 14
        # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: resources
properties.shortDescription: CPU, memory, and compute engine for the backend container.
properties.longDescription:
Defaults to { cpu: 0.5, memory: 1024 }. Override this for production traffic:

  • Hobby / small dev: { cpu: 0.5, memory: 1024 } — fine for a few dozen concurrent users
  • Production baseline: { cpu: 1, memory: 2048 } — handles hundreds of concurrent reactive subscribers
  • Heavier production: { cpu: 2, memory: 4096 } or { cpu: 4, memory: 8192 } — thousands of subscribers, vector search

For EC2 instead of Fargate, specify instanceTypes (e.g., ['c6g.large']). EC2 is typically cheaper per vCPU and supports enableWarmPool: true for faster cold-starts.

Convex backend is single-process — scale vertically (bigger box), not horizontally.

examples.code:
resources:
  backend:
    type: convex
    properties:
      appDirectory: ./convex
      backend:
        # [!code focus-start]
        resources:
          cpu: 4
          memory: 8192
          architecture: arm64
        # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: cloud
properties.shortDescription: API + WebSocket origin. Set as CONVEX_CLOUD_ORIGIN on the backend.
properties.longDescription: Frontend clients connect here via the convex-js client. Example: api.myapp.com.

examples.code:
resources:
  backend:
    type: convex
    properties:
      appDirectory: ./convex
      customDomains:
        # [!code focus-start]
        cloud:
          domainName: api.myapp.com
        # [!code focus-end]
        site:
          domainName: webhooks.myapp.com

properties.name: site
properties.shortDescription: HTTP-actions origin. Set as CONVEX_SITE_ORIGIN on the backend.
properties.longDescription: User-defined httpAction() routes (webhooks, OAuth callbacks) are served here. Example: webhooks.myapp.com.

examples.code:
resources:
  backend:
    type: convex
    properties:
      appDirectory: ./convex
      customDomains:
        cloud:
          domainName: api.myapp.com
        # [!code focus-start]
        site:
          domainName: webhooks.myapp.com
        # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: dashboard
properties.shortDescription: Dashboard domain. Required if dashboard.enabled is true.
properties.longDescription: Example: convex-admin.myapp.com.

examples.code:

  backend:
    type: convex
    properties:

properties.name: allowedIpRanges
properties.shortDescription: CIDR ranges allowed to reach the dashboard. By default the dashboard is internet-reachable.
properties.longDescription:
The dashboard has no built-in authentication — the admin key (which you paste on login) is the only security barrier. Convex's admin key is high-entropy and is the same model managed Convex uses, but if you want defense-in-depth, pin access to your office IPs or VPN range.

Example: allowedIpRanges: ['203.0.113.0/24', '198.51.100.42/32'].

properties.longDescription: The dashboard is a small stateless Next.js app (~$3–5/month at default sizing) that gives you a data browser, log viewer, function REPL, env-var manager, and snapshot export/import UI. Disable only if you have a strong reason — self-hosted Convex without the dashboard is operationally painful.

properties.shortDescription: Pinned Convex dashboard Docker image.
properties.longDescription: Defaults to a known-good version pinned by Stacktape (currently from ghcr.io/get-convex/convex-dashboard). Override to test newer/older versions.

properties.name: metric
properties.shortDescription: The metric to monitor on the Load Balancer.
properties.longDescription:
The threshold will be compared against the calculated value of statistic(METRIC), where:

  • statistic is the function applied to the metric values collected during the evaluation period (default: avg).
  • METRIC is the chosen metric.

Available Metrics:

  • ActiveConnectionCount: The total number of concurrent TCP connections active from clients to the load balancer and from the load balancer to targets.
  • AnomalousHostCount: The number of hosts detected with anomalies.
  • ClientTLSNegotiationErrorCount: The number of TLS connections initiated by the client that did not establish a session with the load balancer due to a TLS error.
  • ConsumedLCUs: The number of load balancer capacity units (LCU) used by your load balancer.
  • DesyncMitigationMode_NonCompliant_Request_Count: The number of requests that do not comply with RFC 7230.
  • DroppedInvalidHeaderRequestCount: The number of requests where the load balancer removed HTTP headers with invalid fields before routing the request.
  • MitigatedHostCount: The number of targets under mitigation.
  • ForwardedInvalidHeaderRequestCount: The number of requests routed by the load balancer that had HTTP headers with invalid fields.
  • GrpcRequestCount: The number of gRPC requests processed over IPv4 and IPv6.
  • HTTP_Fixed_Response_Count: The number of successful fixed-response actions.
  • HTTP_Redirect_Count: The number of successful redirect actions.
  • HTTP_Redirect_Url_Limit_Exceeded_Count: The number of redirect actions that failed because the URL in the response location header exceeded 8K.
  • HTTPCode_ELB_3XX_Count: The number of HTTP 3XX redirection codes originating from the load balancer.
  • HTTPCode_ELB_4XX_Count: The number of HTTP 4XX client error codes originating from the load balancer.
  • HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count: The number of HTTP 5XX server error codes originating from the load balancer.
  • HTTPCode_ELB_500_Count: The number of HTTP 500 error codes originating from the load balancer.
  • HTTPCode_ELB_502_Count: The number of HTTP 502 error codes originating from the load balancer.
  • HTTPCode_ELB_503_Count: The number of HTTP 503 error codes originating from the load balancer.
  • HTTPCode_ELB_504_Count: The number of HTTP 504 error codes originating from the load balancer.
  • IPv6ProcessedBytes: The total number of bytes processed by the load balancer over IPv6.
  • IPv6RequestCount: The number of IPv6 requests received by the load balancer.
  • NewConnectionCount: The total number of new TCP connections established from clients to the load balancer and from the load balancer to targets.
  • NonStickyRequestCount: The number of requests where the load balancer chose a new target because it could not use an existing sticky session.
  • ProcessedBytes: The total number of bytes processed by the load balancer over IPv4 and IPv6.
  • RejectedConnectionCount: The number of connections rejected because the load balancer reached its maximum number of connections.
  • RequestCount: The number of requests processed over IPv4 and IPv6.
  • RuleEvaluations: The number of rules processed by the load balancer, averaged over an hour.
  • HealthyHostCount: The number of targets that are considered healthy.
  • HTTPCode_Target_2XX_Count: The number of HTTP 2XX response codes generated by the targets.
  • HTTPCode_Target_3XX_Count: The number of HTTP 3XX response codes generated by the targets.
  • HTTPCode_Target_4XX_Count: The number of HTTP 4XX response codes generated by the targets.
  • HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count: The number of HTTP 5XX response codes generated by the targets.
  • RequestCountPerTarget: The average number of requests per target in a target group.
  • TargetConnectionErrorCount: The number of connections that were not successfully established between the load balancer and a target.
  • TargetResponseTime: The time elapsed (in seconds) from when a request leaves the load balancer until the target starts sending response headers.
  • TargetTLSNegotiationErrorCount: The number of TLS connections initiated by the load balancer that did not establish a session with the target.
  • UnHealthyHostCount: The number of targets that are considered unhealthy.
  • HealthyStateDNS: The number of zones that meet the DNS healthy state requirements.
  • HealthyStateRouting: The number of zones that meet the routing healthy state requirements.
  • UnhealthyRoutingRequestCount: The number of requests routed using the routing failover action (fail open).
  • UnhealthyStateDNS: The number of zones that do not meet the DNS healthy state requirements.
  • UnhealthyStateRouting: The number of zones that do not meet the routing healthy state requirements.
  • LambdaInternalError: The number of requests to a Lambda function that failed due to an issue internal to the load balancer or AWS Lambda.
  • LambdaTargetProcessedBytes: The total number of bytes processed by the load balancer for requests to and responses from a Lambda function.
  • LambdaUserError: The number of requests to a Lambda function that failed due to an issue with the Lambda function itself.
  • ELBAuthError: The number of user authentications that could not be completed due to an internal error.
  • ELBAuthFailure: The number of user authentications that could not be completed because the IdP denied access.
  • ELBAuthLatency: The time elapsed (in milliseconds) to query the IdP for the ID token and user info.
  • ELBAuthRefreshTokenSuccess: The number of times the load balancer successfully refreshed user claims using a refresh token.

properties.name: customDomains
properties.shortDescription: Custom domains for the Convex backend.
properties.longDescription:
Convex exposes two distinct origins that the outside world reaches:

  • cloud — the API + WebSocket endpoint (CONVEX_CLOUD_ORIGIN). All client traffic (queries, mutations, actions, reactive subscriptions) hits this URL via the convex-js client. Required.
  • site — the HTTP-actions endpoint (CONVEX_SITE_ORIGIN). User-defined httpAction() routes (webhooks, OAuth callbacks, etc.) live here. Kept separate from cloud so webhook URLs don't collide with internal API paths. Required.
  • dashboard — required when dashboard.enabled is true. The dashboard serves at this domain.

Each domain must have a Route53 hosted zone in your AWS account. Stacktape provisions free TLS certificates and DNS records automatically.

If customDomains is omitted entirely, the ALB's default DNS is used with port-based routing (3210 cloud, 3211 site, 6791 dashboard). Fine for dev/staging; not recommended for production — the ALB DNS is unstable across stack recreations, and clients hard-code the URL.

examples.code:
resources:
  backend:
    type: convex
    properties:
      appDirectory: ./convex
      dashboard:
        enabled: true
      # [!code focus-start]
      customDomains:
        cloud:
          domainName: api.myapp.com
        site:
          domainName: webhooks.myapp.com
        dashboard:
          domainName: convex-admin.myapp.com
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: dashboard
properties.shortDescription: Configuration for the Convex admin dashboard.
properties.longDescription: Enabled by default. The dashboard is a stateless Next.js app that talks to the backend's REST API using the admin key (which you paste on first login). To opt out, set dashboard.enabled: false.

examples.code:
resources:
  backend:
    type: convex
    properties:
      appDirectory: ./convex
      # [!code focus-start]
      dashboard:
        enabled: true
        allowedIpRanges:
          - 203.0.113.0/24
        resources:
          cpu: 0.25
          memory: 512
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: database
properties.shortDescription: Override the PostgreSQL database that backs the Convex deployment.
properties.longDescription:
Defaults to a single-AZ RDS PostgreSQL db.t4g.micro instance (cheapest production-viable option, ~$13/month). The shape mirrors a subset of relational-database — override only what you need. Common reasons to override: bump to Aurora Serverless v2 for auto-scaling, enable multi-AZ for HA, or increase storage retention.

You cannot bring an existing external database — Convex assumes it owns its Postgres entirely.

examples.code:
resources:
  backend:
    type: convex
    properties:
      appDirectory: ./convex
      # [!code focus-start]
      database:
        engine:
          type: aurora-postgresql-serverless-v2
          properties:
            version: '16.6'
            minCapacity: 0.5
            maxCapacity: 4
        automatedBackupRetentionDays: 7
      # [!code focus-end]

properties.name: deletionProtection
properties.shortDescription: Prevent accidental deletion of the database and the five storage buckets.
properties.longDescription:
When true, Stacktape sets deletionProtection on the underlying RDS instance and retention policies on the buckets. You must set this to false and redeploy before you can delete the stack.

Recommended for production stages.

      # [!code focus-end]

properties.shortDescription: Dev mode: runs the convex-backend locally in Docker by default with SQLite + local filesystem storage.
properties.longDescription: Set remote: true to point stacktape dev at the deployed AWS backend instead. Local mode is recommended because Convex's save-push-reload loop is noticeably faster over loopback than across the WAN, and avoids 24/7 Fargate + RDS cost per developer.

properties.shortDescription: How Stacktape deploys Convex functions after infrastructure is ready.

By default, Stacktape runs npx convex deploy --codegen disable --typecheck try from the project directory containing appDirectory, with CONVEX_SELF_HOSTED_URL and CONVEX_SELF_HOSTED_ADMIN_KEY injected automatically.

Set enabled: false if your CI/CD pipeline deploys functions separately, or set command when your project uses a custom package-manager command.
